Look at dxc_trunk vs dxc_1_6_2112 (an old release) side by side.

dxc_1_6_2112 (old): compiles cleanly. The disassembly it emits contains
`zext i32 %N to i33` / `mul i33 ...` / `trunc i33 %N to i32` -- SCEV has
widened the loop's overflow-guarded closed-form multiply
((input-1)*(input-2))/2 by one bit, past DXIL's supported integer widths
(i1/i8/i16/i32/i64). The extra bit is silently baked into the module; only
the disassembly text gives it away.

dxc_trunk (current): fails with `error: Int type 'i33' has an invalid
width.`. The same SCEV widening still happens internally (confirmed
locally with -Vd, which skips validation) -- what changed is that the
DXIL validator's Types.IntWidth rule now catches it and refuses to run
instead of letting it through.

So this is not fixed: the root defect (the illegal i33 induction-variable
type) is present on every dxc release tested, from v1.4.1907 through
current main. What changed recently (between the v1.9.2602.24 and
v1.9.2607 releases) is that the validator started rejecting it, turning a
previously-silent correctness bug into a hard compile failure.
